title: Spatially resolved quantum magnetometry and stray-field reconstruction of permalloy microdisks using boron-vacancy centers in hexagonal boron nitride
authors: Peiting Wen, Shuyu Wen, Jiang Qu, Zeling Xiong, Katrin Schultheiss, Slawomir Prucnal, Artur Erbe, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jürgen Lindner, Jürgen Fassbender, Manfred Helm, Shengqiang Zhou, Ruslan Salikhov, Helmut Schultheiss, Yonder Berencén
abstract: Transferable hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) hosting negatively charged boron-vacancy (VB$^{-}$) spin defects offers a versatile platform for integrated quantum magnetometry, yet quantitative imaging of magnetic microstructures remains challenging. Here, we integrate a transferred hBN flake with a 4 $μ$m-diameter permalloy (Py = Ni${81}$Fe${19}$) microdisk and perform spatially resolved optically detected magnetic resonance measurements at room temperature. An applied in-plane magnetic field distorts the vortex-state magnetization, generating edge-localized magnetic surface charges and pronounced stray-field signatures at opposite disk edges. By referencing each pixel to its local zero-field splitting and correcting for a residual out-of-plane bias field, we quantitatively reconstruct the out-of-plane stray-field distribution, revealing peak fields of approximately 11.2 mT. An edge-charge model reproduces the spatial distribution and amplitude of the reconstructed field, linking the ODMR response to the field-driven evolution of the vortex state. These results establish transferred hBN VB$^{-}$ sensors for quantitative magnetometry of magnetic microstructures.
summary: This study reports on a novel method for quantitative magnetometry by integrating boron-vacancy spin defects in hBN onto permalloy microdisks. Using spatially resolved ODMR measurements, the researchers successfully reconstructed the out-of-plane stray magnetic field from a vortex-state disk. This validates the use of hBN quantum defects as highly sensitive, room-temperature sensors for mapping magnetic textures.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of quantitatively imaging magnetic microstructures, specifically the stray-field distribution from permalloy microdisks, using spatially resolved quantum magnetometry.
main_result: The authors successfully reconstructed the out-of-plane stray-field distribution, revealing peak fields of approximately 11.2 mT, and validated this reconstruction using an edge-charge model.
method: Spatially resolved Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) measurements were performed on boron-vacancy (VB-) spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) integrated with the magnetic sample.
model_or_system: The system involves a permalloy microdisk exhibiting a vortex state, measured using VB- centers in hBN. The analysis relies on relating the measured ODMR splitting to the local magnetic field via established quantum resonance equations.
key_observables: Reconstructed out-of-plane stray-field distribution ($	ext{B}_z$), ODMR transition frequencies ($f_-, f_+$), and the magnetic-field-dependent splitting parameters ($D$ and $E$).
important_parameters: Peak stray field $\approx 11.2 	ext{ mT}$; measurement temperature (room temperature); sensor sensitivity ($\approx 100 \mu	ext{T}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that local variations in the ODMR parameters can be separated into contributions from intrinsic spin properties (strain) and the external magnetic field.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup, ODMR spectra used for fitting, the reconstructed magnitude and signed distribution of the stray field, and comparisons between the reconstructed field and predictions from the edge-charge model.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of establishing the platform (hBN/VB- sensor), detailing the measurement technique (ODMR), applying the technique to a specific magnetic problem (Py disk vortex state), and finally quantitatively reconstructing the stray field using theoretical models (edge-charge model) for validation.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a powerful, room-temperature quantum sensing modality for mapping magnetic fields, bridging quantum defect physics with classical condensed matter magnetism, which is highly relevant for quantum sensing applications.
